brief: Hype cycles, and telling a real shift from a loud one

slots.eyebrow: On telling a shift from a noise
slots.standfirst: Once as an announcement that changes nothing, and years later as a quiet change nobody announced. Six ways to tell which one you are looking at.
slots.item1: Deciding whether to spend a quarter on something everybody is talking about.
slots.item2: Tell you which specific thing wins. Nothing does that, including the winners.
slots.coverNote: The last one is why being early is usually indistinguishable from being wrong

slots.titleLine1: Follow the users, not the conference.
slots.body: A real shift shows up first in people quietly changing what they do, and a loud one shows up first in people explaining what everybody should do. The gap between those two populations is the single most reliable signal available.
slots.g1: Not who is excited. Who has actually stopped doing the old thing.
slots.g2: Anybody whose income depends on the shift is not evidence of it.
slots.g3: The unglamorous adopters are the ones with a real problem.
slots.g4: Trying something is free. Abandoning what you had is not.

slots.titleLine1: New things win by being cheaper at something.
slots.body: Every shift that held displaced a specific existing cost — in money, time, or people needed. If nobody can say precisely what is now unnecessary, the thing is an addition to the stack rather than a change in it, and additions do not stick.
slots.g1: In a sentence, with a number, or it has not been displaced.
slots.g2: Cost pushed to another team is a reorganisation, not a saving.
slots.g3: Ten per cent cheaper is a feature. Ten times is a shift.
slots.g4: Real change is visible in what stops existing, not what starts.

slots.titleLine1: The timeline is always longer and the effect larger.
slots.body: Almost every genuine shift takes about three times as long as its advocates say and ends up bigger than its sceptics allow. Both errors are structural rather than accidental, which means you can correct for them in advance without knowing anything else.
slots.g1: By three, whoever gave it and however conservative they claimed to be.
slots.g2: The trough between announcement and adoption looks exactly like failure.
slots.g3: The companies that matter usually arrive after the first cohort dies.
slots.g4: Nothing about the loudest month predicts anything about year four.

slots.sectionLabel: What it costs to be wrong
slots.titleLine1: Ask what you lose in each direction.
slots.body: The interesting question is not which way the shift goes but what happens to you if you guess wrong either way. Most of the time the two costs are wildly different, and the asymmetry decides the question without needing a forecast at all.
slots.g1: Adopting a dud and missing a real one are rarely comparable.
slots.g2: A cheap wrong bet you can unwind beats a correct one you cannot.
slots.g3: Small deliberate exposure costs little and removes the need to be right.
slots.g4: The cost of being wrong is mostly the cost of getting back out.

slots.titleLine1: Most of your work is not affected.
slots.body: Even genuine shifts change one layer and leave the rest untouched, and the mistake is treating a real change in one place as a general change everywhere. Naming the specific layer is the difference between adapting and rebuilding things that were fine.
slots.g1: Which specific step changes. Everything above and below probably does not.
slots.g2: A new foundation rarely justifies replacing what was standing on it.
slots.g3: What connects the parts outlives whatever is behind any one of them.
slots.g4: Two at once and you cannot tell which decision was the mistake.

slots.titleLine1: Early and wrong look identical for years.
slots.body: There is no test that separates a correct early call from a mistaken one until the thing either happens or does not. Everybody who was right about something big spent a long period indistinguishable from the people who were simply wrong.
slots.g1: No amount of analysis resolves it before the outcome does.
slots.g2: Conviction you cannot verify should not be funded like conviction you can.
slots.g3: Decided in advance, so the review is not an argument about feelings.
slots.g4: Publicly, on the record. Otherwise you will quietly move the target.

slots.eyebrow: On the thing everybody is currently sure about
slots.body: One sentence, one specific cost that disappears. If you cannot write it, the thing is an addition rather than a shift, whatever the volume around it.
slots.closingLine: Nothing that only adds has ever changed anything, and almost everything loud only adds.
slots.signoff: Then set a date to check
